Olduvai Gorge. A ravine in Tanzania containing some of the world's most important fossil evidence of human evolution and early stone tool manufacture, spanning roughly two million years of human prehistory. Systematic excavations beginning in 1931 uncovered remains of human ancestors and Homo habilis, along with the earliest known stone tools of the Oldowan industry, fundamentally reshaping understanding of human origins and the African genesis of our species.

Located in northern Tanzania near the Serengeti, Olduvai Gorge is a thirty-mile-long ravine carved by the Olduvai River through multiple geological layers dating back two million years. The site was excavated primarily by the Leakey family—Louis, Mary, and Richard Leakey—whose discoveries over seven decades of fieldwork revolutionized the field of paleoanthropology.

The gorge contains fossils of Homo habilis, meaning "handy man," the earliest known member of the genus Homo, dated to approximately 2.3 million years ago. The Oldowan stone tool industry consists of simple flakes and choppers made by striking one stone against another—the earliest evidence that tool-making preceded modern human anatomy. These discoveries provided crucial evidence that human evolution occurred in Africa, contrary to earlier European-centric theories, establishing Africa as the birthplace of humankind.

Multiple hominin species are represented in the fossil record at Olduvai, including Australopithecus, Homo habilis, and Homo erectus, spanning the transition from ape-like ancestors to modern humans. The exceptional preservation of fossils and tools occurs because volcanic ash repeatedly blanketed the site, preventing decay and creating clear temporal markers. Through Olduvai Gorge, we read the fossil record foundation that explains how humans arose from earlier primates.
